```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
art <- here::here("SciRep_emotions_in_working_donkeys_Bukhari_2026")
rd  <- function(p) read_csv(file.path(art, p), show_col_types = FALSE, progress = FALSE)
f   <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(round(x, d), format = "f", digits = d)
t2c <- rd("data/raw/table2_conditions.csv")
t2d <- rd("data/raw/table2_changes.csv")
cc  <- rd("output/tables/consistency_contrasts.csv")
sbs <- rd("output/tables/stage4_side_by_side.csv")
e5  <- rd("output/tables/stage4_e5_auc.csv")
T2  <- function(o, cnd) t2c$mean[t2c$outcome == o & t2c$condition == cnd]
D2  <- function(o, t) t2d$delta_mean[t2d$outcome == o & t2d$treatment == t]
S   <- function(o, term, scale) sbs$stage4[sbs$outcome == o & sbs$term == term & sbs$scale == scale & sbs$rho_dd == 0][1]
A   <- function(contrast, quantity, w = "estimate") e5[[w]][e5$model == "sbr_nb2" & e5$rho_dd == 0 & e5$contrast == contrast & e5$quantity == quantity][1]
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This page explains, without statistics, what the [technical review](review.qmd) of Bukhari and
colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2026) found. The review is the reference; this page is a guide to it.
The authors have been contacted and their reply will be published with the review.
:::

## What the study did

Thirty-four working donkeys in Pakistan were each filmed and measured for three minutes in three
situations: standing quietly as usual (the control), eating fresh lucerne from a bucket (meant to be a
pleasant experience) and hearing hair clippers held close to one ear (meant to be an unpleasant one).
Three things were measured each time: how often the donkey blinked, the temperature of the inner corner
of its eye, and a heart-rhythm measure called RMSSD that tends to be higher when an animal is relaxed.

The authors report that blinking went up with the lucerne and down with the clippers, that eye temperature
went up in both situations, and that RMSSD went up in both situations too. They conclude that the three
measures "may act as indicators of emotions in donkeys" and suggest that blink rate could be a simple
field test of how a donkey feels.

## What we did

We read the paper against a fixed checklist, recomputed every number that can be recomputed from the
tables, recovered the individual data points that the paper plots in two of its figures, and rebuilt
complete datasets consistent with everything the paper reports. On those we refitted the authors' own
analysis and then a better-specified one, twice over with two different statistical approaches, to see
what the design can actually tell us. All of this is code in a public repository, and the authors have
been asked for the original data so that the same code can be run on them.

## What we found, area by area

The checklist looks at six areas. The table counts the problems recorded in each; the technical
review lists every one of them with its evidence.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-quality-plain
#| tbl-cap: "Problems found, by area. A problem is 'settled by the paper's own numbers' when no assumption and no extra data are needed to see it; the others depend on a stated assumption or on the original data. 'Serious' means it affects a conclusion of the paper."
source(here::here("lib/quality_table.R"))
plain_area <- c("Design" = "How the study was set up", "Measurement" = "What was measured, and how",
                "Model adequacy" = "How the data were analysed",
                "Internal consistency" = "Whether the numbers agree with each other",
                "Reporting" = "How it was reported", "Inference" = "What was concluded")
plain_rating <- c("conclusions at risk" = "puts the conclusions at risk", "major concerns" = "serious",
                  "minor concerns" = "minor", "no concern found" = "none found")
quality_table("P001") |>
  transmute(Area = unname(plain_area[Domain]),
            `Problems found` = Critical + Major + Minor,
            `Of which serious` = Critical + Major,
            `Settled by the paper's own numbers` = Confirmed,
            `Our reading` = unname(plain_rating[Rating])) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe", align = "lrrrl")
```

## Five things a reader should know

**1. The "changes" in the paper have lost their sign.** The authors define each change as the control
value minus the treatment value. By that definition, when a measure goes *up* under a treatment the
change is negative. Five of the six changes in the paper should be negative; all six are printed as
positive numbers. Working back from the figures, the printed changes are the sizes of the per-donkey
changes with the direction removed. That matters because the paper's second analysis, which relates the
heart measure to blinking and to eye temperature, was run on these direction-free numbers, and the text
then talks about "the direction of change" becoming "more obvious".

**2. Two of the p-values cannot come from the data as reported.** A p-value is a way of saying how
surprising a result would be if nothing were going on. For the blink rate under lucerne the paper
reports p = `{r} f(cc$p_reported[cc$outcome == "SBR" & cc$treatment == "positive"], 3)`. From the paper's
own averages and spreads, the effect is so large (every donkey blinked more, by about
`{r} f(D2("SBR", "positive"), 0)` blinks a minute on an average of `{r} f(T2("SBR", "control"), 0)`) that the
p-value should be smaller by many orders of magnitude. The same holds for the heart measure under
lucerne. Whatever produced those two numbers, it was not the analysis the paper describes applied to the
data the paper summarises. This is a statement about the numbers, not about anyone's intentions; a
transcription slip or an undescribed analysis step would both produce it.

**3. The discussion says one result went the opposite way from what the results show.** The paper's
Discussion states that the heart measure *fell* under the clippers, "consistent with previous studies in
horses". Its own Table 2 shows it *rose*, from `{r} f(T2("RMSSD", "control"), 0)` to
`{r} f(T2("RMSSD", "negative"), 0)` milliseconds, and its own figure marks that rise as highly significant.
This is the sentence on which the claim that heart rhythm tells pleasant from unpleasant rests.

**4. The comparison the conclusions need was never made.** To say that a measure distinguishes a
pleasant from an unpleasant experience, you have to compare the two experiences with each other. The
paper only compares each of them with standing quietly. For eye temperature and the heart measure, both
experiences pushed the measure the same way; what differs is how far. A thermometer that reads higher
whether the donkey is pleased or frightened cannot tell you which it is.

**5. Nothing shows the donkeys felt what the labels say.** The lucerne is assumed pleasant and the
clippers unpleasant, which is reasonable, but nothing independent was recorded to check it: no behaviour
beyond blinking, no heart rate, no sign of approach or avoidance. And the "pleasant" situation is eating.
Chewing and a head down in a bucket change breathing, heart rhythm, and what a camera pointed at the eye
can see, whatever the donkey feels about it. The study cannot separate "eating" from "happy".

## What our re-analysis shows

With a model suited to the kind of data (counts for blinks, a skewed positive quantity for the heart
measure, each donkey's three values analysed together), fitted two ways with the same result:

- **Blinking does separate the three situations**, and in opposite directions: about
  `{r} S("SBR", "positive - control", "difference (blinks/min)")` blinks a minute more with lucerne and
  `{r} S("SBR", "negative - control", "difference (blinks/min)")` fewer with the clippers (the numbers in
  brackets are the range we are fairly confident the true value lies in). This is the one claim of the
  paper that the data clearly support.
- **Eye temperature and the heart measure rose in both situations.** The two treatments do differ from
  each other in how much (eye temperature `{r} S("ET", "positive - negative", "difference (degC)")` °C,
  heart measure `{r} S("RMSSD", "positive - negative", "difference (ms, marginal)")` milliseconds, lucerne
  minus clippers), but a difference in how far a needle moves in the same direction is not a
  direction.
- **The link between blinking and heart rhythm has opposite signs in the two situations.** With lucerne,
  donkeys that blinked more also had a higher heart measure; with the clippers, donkeys that blinked less
  did. The paper's single combined slope averages these two opposite relations.
- **As a field test for one donkey**, a single blink count tells lucerne from clippers almost perfectly
  (the chance that a random "lucerne" reading beats a random "clipper" reading is
  `{r} f(A("positive vs negative", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)`, where 0.5 would be a coin toss), and
  lucerne from calm well (`{r} f(A("positive vs control", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)`). It tells
  clippers from calm only moderately (`{r} f(A("control vs negative", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)`): at the
  best cut-off of `{r} f(A("control vs negative", "best threshold (reading >= t called A)"), 0)` blinks a
  minute, about one reading in four is misclassified either way. The part of the claim most useful in
  practice, spotting a stressed donkey from its blinking, is the weak one.

Everything in this section rests on data rebuilt from the paper's figures and tables, not on the
original records, and the review says so at each step. If the authors share their data, the same code
runs on them and this page will be updated.

### The numbers side by side

The same results as a table. The paper's numbers are as printed; ours are the central estimate with,
in brackets, the range we are fairly confident the true value lies in (the technical review has the
full version of this table, with what each quantity is).

| What was compared | The paper's number | Our number | In plain words |
|:----------|:--------|:--------|:--------------|
| Blinks, lucerne vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("SBR", "positive"), 1)` per minute (printed without a direction) | `{r} S("SBR", "positive - control", "difference (blinks/min)")` per minute | A donkey eating lucerne blinks about twice as often (`{r} S("SBR", "positive / control", "ratio")` times) |
| Blinks, clippers vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("SBR", "negative"), 1)` per minute (printed as a positive number) | `{r} S("SBR", "negative - control", "difference (blinks/min)")` per minute | About a third fewer blinks |
| Blinks, lucerne vs clippers | not compared | `{r} S("SBR", "positive - negative", "difference (blinks/min)")` per minute | Three times as many blinks with lucerne as with the clippers; the one clear opposite-direction result |
| Eye temperature, lucerne vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("ET", "positive"), 2)` °C | `{r} S("ET", "positive - control", "difference (degC)")` °C | The eye warms |
| Eye temperature, clippers vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("ET", "negative"), 2)` °C | `{r} S("ET", "negative - control", "difference (degC)")` °C | The eye warms here too, a little more |
| Eye temperature, lucerne vs clippers | not compared; described as a difference in emotion | `{r} S("ET", "positive - negative", "difference (degC)")` °C | A difference in how much, not in which direction |
| Heart measure, lucerne vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("RMSSD", "positive"), 1)` ms | `{r} S("RMSSD", "positive - control", "difference (ms, marginal)")` ms | Goes up |
| Heart measure, clippers vs quiet | `{r} f(D2("RMSSD", "negative"), 1)` ms (the discussion calls it a fall) | `{r} S("RMSSD", "negative - control", "difference (ms, marginal)")` ms | Goes up as well, not down |
| Heart measure, lucerne vs clippers | not compared | `{r} S("RMSSD", "positive - negative", "difference (ms, marginal)")` ms | Both up; lucerne more |
| Blinks and heart measure together | one slope for both situations | lucerne `{r} S("E4 (x = dSBR)", "b (slope), positive", "response")`, clippers `{r} S("E4 (x = dSBR)", "b (slope), negative", "response")` ms per blink | The link runs one way with lucerne and the opposite way with the clippers; averaging them hides both |
| One blink count as a field test | proposed, not tested | lucerne vs clippers `{r} f(A("positive vs negative", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)`, lucerne vs quiet `{r} f(A("positive vs control", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)`, quiet vs clippers `{r} f(A("control vs negative", "AUC, different donkeys"), 2)` | Chance that a reading from one state beats a reading from the other (0.5 is a coin toss): near-certain for lucerne vs clippers, three times in four for quiet vs clippers |

## What this does and does not mean

It does not mean the donkeys felt nothing, nor that blink rate is useless. It means that this paper, as
published, does not support its claims about eye temperature and heart rhythm as markers of pleasant
versus unpleasant emotion, and that its numbers are not internally consistent in ways the authors should
be able to resolve with their data. The group-level finding about blinking stands on the reported
numbers and on our re-analysis.

Methods and numbers are criticised here, never people. The authors received a data request and notice
of this commentary before anything was written, will receive the full text before it is published, and
their reply will appear alongside it.
